The numbers 1, 2, ..., 2100 are written on a board. Every second, Mark takes two numbers on the board, \( a \) and \( b \), erases them, and replaces them with \( \gcd(a, b) \) and \( \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) \). Mark stops once any move he makes will not change the numbers written on the board. Compute the number of divisors of the 2026th smallest positive integer written on the board when he finishes.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let \(n=2100\). For a positive integer \(x\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of prime \(p\) in \(x\).

When Mark replaces \(a,b\) by \(\gcd(a,b)\) and \(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\), for each prime \(p\) the exponents
\[
(v_p(a),v_p(b))
\]
are replaced by
\[
(\min(v_p(a),v_p(b)),\max(v_p(a),v_p(b))).
\]
Thus, for every prime \(p\), the multiset of \(p\)-adic exponents on the board is invariant.

When Mark stops, every possible move changes nothing. That means for any two board numbers \(a,b\),
\[
\{\gcd(a,b),\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\}=\{a,b\},
\]
which happens exactly when one of \(a,b\) divides the other. So the final board is a chain under divisibility.

Sort the final board as
\[
x_1\mid x_2\mid \cdots \mid x_{2100}.
\]
For each prime \(p\), the sequence \(v_p(x_1),v_p(x_2),\dots,v_p(x_{2100})\) is nondecreasing. Since its multiset is invariant, it must be the sorted list of the initial exponents
\[
v_p(1),v_p(2),\dots,v_p(2100).
\]
Therefore the \(2026\)th smallest final number is determined by, for each prime \(p\), the \(2026\)th smallest exponent among \(v_p(1),\dots,v_p(2100)\).

For a fixed prime \(p\) and integer \(e\ge 0\), the number of integers \(m\le 2100\) with \(v_p(m)\le e\) is
\[
2100-\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^{e+1}}\right\rfloor,
\]
because the integers with \(v_p(m)\ge e+1\) are exactly the multiples of \(p^{e+1}\).

We need this to be at least \(2026\):
\[
2100-\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^{e+1}}\right\rfloor \ge 2026
\]
\[
\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^{e+1}}\right\rfloor \le 74.
\]
Since
\[
\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{q}\right\rfloor\le 74 \iff q\ge 29,
\]
we need the smallest \(e\) such that
\[
p^{e+1}\ge 29.
\]

Now compute the relevant exponents:

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccccc}
p & 2 & 3 & 5 & 7 & 11 & 13 & 17 & 19 & 23 & \ge 29\\
\hline
e_p & 4 & 3 & 2 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 0
\end{array}
\]

Thus the \(2026\)th smallest final number is
\[
2^4\cdot 3^3\cdot 5^2\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13\cdot 17\cdot 19\cdot 23.
\]

Its number of positive divisors is
\[
(4+1)(3+1)(2+1)(1+1)^6
=5\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 64
=3840.
\]

\[
\boxed{3840}
\]
